summary: A constitutional monarchy on the Iberian Peninsula that once built a colonial empire spanning the globe, known for its diverse regional cultures, art and cuisine.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Christianity reached the Iberian Peninsula in Roman times, and in 589 the Visigothic king Reccared converted to Catholicism at the Third Council of Toledo. After the Muslim conquest of most of the peninsula in 711, the northern Christian kingdoms launched the “Reconquista,” taking Granada in 1492; the Catholic Monarchs then expelled the Jews, and together with the Inquisition (established in 1478) and the expulsion of the Moriscos in 1609, this made Catholicism the only faith. From 1939 to 1975 Franco promoted “National Catholicism,” and only the 1978 constitution established a non-confessional state, after which the share of believers has continued to decline.

ranking.name: No religion (including atheism and agnosticism)
ranking.description: After the end of the Franco dictatorship, Spain democratized and modernized rapidly in the 1980s, the Church’s influence over education and morality declined greatly, and reforms such as the legalization of same-sex marriage in 2005 symbolized the society’s secular turn. Among the younger generation, those who identify as atheist or agnostic now exceed half, and many take part in religious activities only on cultural occasions such as weddings, funerals or Holy Week processions.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: From 711 to 1492 Islam ruled in al-Andalus for centuries, but it almost disappeared after the Moriscos were expelled in the early 17th century. Today’s Muslims come mainly from the large wave of Moroccan immigrants since the 1990s and from residents of the North African enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla, concentrated in Catalonia, Andalusia and Madrid.

ranking.name: Other (Protestant, Orthodox, etc.)
ranking.description: Protestantism was severely suppressed by the Inquisition in the 16th century and gained full freedom only after democratization; the evangelical “Filadelfia Church,” which arose among the Roma from the 1950s, has a large following. Large numbers of Romanian immigrants in the 2000s brought Orthodoxy, making it an important minority religion.

religion.background: Spain’s religious history is inseparable from the formation of the state: in the Middle Ages Christians, Muslims and Jews coexisted and clashed on the Iberian Peninsula, and after the reconquest of Granada and the expulsion of the Jews in 1492, Catholicism became a symbol of national unity, with the Inquisition ensuring uniformity of belief. In the 19th and 20th centuries liberals and the Church were long opposed; in the Spanish Civil War (1936–1939) the Church supported Franco, and after the war Catholicism again became the state religion. The democratic constitution of 1978 separated church and state, after which Spain secularized rapidly, while immigrants brought Islam and Orthodoxy.

language.official: The official language is Spanish (Castilian); Catalan, Galician and Basque also have official status within their autonomous communities.

ranking.name: Spanish (Castilian)
ranking.description: Castilian originated in the Kingdom of Castile in the north of the Iberian Peninsula in the 9th–10th centuries; in the 13th century Alfonso X used it to compile law codes and histories, and in 1492 Nebrija published the first grammar of Spanish. As Castile led the Reconquista and unified Spain, it became the language of administration and culture for the whole country, and in 1713 the Royal Spanish Academy was founded to regulate the language. Today it is the official language of the whole country and also the common second language of residents of other language regions.

ranking.name: Catalan (including Valencian)
ranking.description: Catalan was an important literary and legal language in the medieval Crown of Aragon. After the War of the Spanish Succession in 1714, the Bourbons issued the Nueva Planta decrees restricting its official use; the Renaixença movement of the 19th century restored its literary standing, but it was banned again under Franco. After 1978 it became a co-official language of Catalonia, Valencia and the Balearic Islands, schools commonly teach in it, and it is closely tied to the identity of the independence movement.

ranking.name: Galician
ranking.description: Galician shares a common origin with Portuguese; medieval “Galician-Portuguese” was the language of lyric poetry on the Iberian Peninsula, and Alfonso X’s Cantigas de Santa Maria were written in it. After the 15th century Castilianization reduced it to a rural spoken language, and in 1863 Rosalía de Castro published Cantares gallegos, which drove a revival; since 1981 it has been a co-official language of the autonomous community of Galicia, and its use in the countryside remains high.

ranking.name: Basque
ranking.description: Basque is the only surviving pre-Indo-European language in Western Europe and has no relation to any known language; it was spoken in the western Pyrenees long before the Romans arrived. It was suppressed under Franco, and was transmitted through underground “Basque-language schools” (ikastolas); a unified written standard was set in 1968, and from 1979 it became a co-official language in the Basque Autonomous Community, with schooling increasing the number of young speakers.

language.history: Roman rule led Latin to replace most of the indigenous languages of the Iberian Peninsula, and only Basque survived. During the al-Andalus period after 711 Arabic had a profound influence, leaving thousands of loanwords (such as words beginning with al-). In the Middle Ages the Latin dialects of the northern kingdoms developed into Castilian, Catalan, Galician and others, and as Castile expanded, Castilian became the language of the whole country and, in the 15th–16th centuries, spread across the Americas with colonization. The Franco era suppressed regional languages, and the 1978 constitution recognized the co-official status of the languages of the autonomous communities.

ranking.name: Paella
ranking.description: Meat or seafood is sautéed in olive oil in a large shallow pan, then saffron, rice and stock are added and cooked until dry, forming a crispy, toasty crust (socarrat) on the bottom of the pan.
ranking.history: Rice was introduced by the Moors in the Middle Ages and grown around the Albufera lagoon near Valencia, and saffron is also a spice brought by the Arabs. In the 19th century Valencian farmers in the countryside cooked rice in large shallow pans in the fields, adding chicken, rabbit and beans, forming the traditional “paella valenciana”; the name comes from the Valencian word “paella” for a frying pan, which can be traced to the Latin patella. The seafood version became widespread only after tourism arose in the 20th century, and Valencians still have the habit of sharing paella with the whole family on Sundays.

ranking.name: Tortilla española (Spanish potato omelet)
ranking.description: Potato slices and onion are slowly fried in plenty of olive oil until soft, then mixed with beaten egg and cooked into a thick round cake that can be cut into pieces and eaten hot or cold.
ranking.history: The potato was brought back to Europe from the Americas by the Spanish in the 16th century and was mostly used as fodder at first, becoming widely eaten as food only in the 18th century. The earliest known records of the tortilla de patatas appear in early 19th-century Navarre, and folk tradition holds that it was invented during the Carlist wars of the 1830s to feed soldiers quickly. Because the ingredients are cheap and it is easy to carry, it has become Spain’s most common tapa, indispensable from bars to family picnics, and whether to add onion is a topic Spaniards argue about endlessly.

ranking.name: Jamón ibérico
ranking.description: A ham made from the hind leg of the Iberian black pig, cured with sea salt and air-dried and matured for two to four years, sliced thin, with fat that melts in the mouth and a nutty aroma.
ranking.history: The Iberian black pig is a breed unique to the Iberian Peninsula, raised free-range on the oak pastures (dehesa) of Extremadura and Andalusia in the southwest and fed on acorns in autumn and winter, which gives it a distinctive flavor. The technique of curing ham already existed in Roman times. After the Reconquista, eating pork for a time became a way of proving oneself a Christian rather than a converted Jew or Muslim, giving ham a particular cultural meaning. Today production areas such as Jabugo and Guijuelo are protected by designation of origin, and ham is a premium food for festivals and entertaining guests.

ranking.name: Gazpacho
ranking.description: Tomato, cucumber, sweet pepper, garlic and day-old bread are blended with olive oil and vinegar into a chilled vegetable soup, refreshing and slightly sour, often drunk straight as a beverage in summer.
ranking.history: Gazpacho originated in the peasant food of Andalusia in the south, and the early version was pounded from bread, garlic, olive oil, vinegar and water, which can be traced to Roman and Moorish traditions. After tomatoes and peppers arrived from the Americas in the 16th century, they became the main ingredients of gazpacho only in the 19th century, forming today’s red version. Andalusian summers are scorching, and gazpacho replenishes fluid and salt, and is a drink commonly kept in the refrigerator of every household there in summer.

ranking.name: Churros
ranking.description: Batter is piped through a star-shaped nozzle into hot oil and fried into long sticks, crisp outside and soft inside, sprinkled with sugar and eaten dipped in thick hot chocolate.
ranking.history: The origin of churros is disputed, one account holding that it was a food of Spanish shepherds who fried batter in the mountains with simple ingredients. Chocolate was brought back to Europe from the Aztecs by the Spanish in the 16th century, thick hot chocolate became popular in the Spanish court and among the people, and it later became a classic pairing with churros. The Chocolatería San Ginés in Madrid, opened in 1894, is still in business, and Spaniards often eat churros with chocolate in the early hours of New Year’s Day after the New Year’s Eve revelry; it also spread to Latin America with colonization.
